analysis.one_liner: Expands federal and state power to investigate police departments for civil rights abuses.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2020, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the Justice Department more money and clearer authority to investigate police departments and prosecutors' offices that show a pattern of violating people's civil rights. It would also let state attorneys general sue those agencies in federal court — a power that currently only the federal Justice Department has — and cancel a 2018 Justice Department policy that made it harder to lock in reform agreements with local police. It died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of cities and states where police departments or prosecutors' offices engage in a pattern of civil rights violations would gain a new path to court-ordered reform: their own state attorney general could sue in federal court without waiting on the federal Justice Department [S2][S3]. State and tribal governments would have access to federal grants to build investigation capacity [S3]. People subject to biased policing would also benefit from the bill's rollback of the 2018 DOJ memo that limited how reform agreements with local governments can be structured [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill authorizes $445 million per year for ten years for the DOJ Civil Rights Division, with at least $100 million per year reserved specifically for pattern-or-practice investigations of law enforcement agencies [S3].

It gives state attorneys general the power to sue law enforcement agencies in federal court over a pattern or practice of depriving people of their civil rights — authority currently held only by DOJ — and lets DOJ issue grants to states and tribal governments to pursue such cases [S2][S3].

It voids a November 2018 Justice Department memo that imposed procedures and limits on civil consent decrees and settlement agreements with state and local governments, which had made long-term reform commitments harder to secure [S2][S3].
It expands the definition of unlawful conduct to include prosecutors and other agencies involved in the administration of justice, not just police departments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on the federal treasury — up to roughly $595 million per year in authorized appropriations — and on law enforcement agencies that would face more investigations and binding reform agreements, which can require changes to training, practices, and oversight [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes very large spending — $445 million plus $150 million per year for a decade — with no offsetting revenue or budget constraint, and authorized appropriations do not guarantee the money is actually provided [S3].

Giving state attorneys general independent power to sue local police agencies could make local departments answer to litigation from their own state officials, raising federalism concerns about state officials prosecuting entities within their own government [S3].

Consent decrees imposed through litigation can be costly for local governments and can leave reform decisions in the hands of courts rather than elected local officials, a genuine cost supporters should acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — a functioning federal pipeline for civil rights investigations, a state-level check on police misconduct, and the removal of a self-imposed DOJ barrier to consent decrees — directly target accountability that was hard to obtain, especially after 2018. The costs are real: significant federal spending and expensive litigation for local governments. The largest design weakness is that the funding is authorization-only and the state enforcement power depends on state attorneys general choosing to use it. On balance it is a straightforward accountability bill whose main costs fall on police agencies that would rather not be investigated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cedric Richmond introduced the bill on July 2, 2020, during the national debate over policing that followed George Floyd's death, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
The bill never advanced beyond that referral: the action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no report, and no floor action [S5].
It attracted only two cosponsors, Reps. Norton and Hastings, giving it very little visible support in the chamber [S4].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and prosecutors' offices that could have faced state-led pattern-or-practice lawsuits or stricter federal consent decrees are better off because the bill died. The 2018 DOJ limits on consent decrees remained in place, and the federal Civil Rights Division received none of the bill's dedicated investigation funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies that avoided new oversight

for.name: Rep. Cedric Richmond
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House

for.name: Reps. Eleanor Holmes Norton and Alcee Hastings

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jerrold Nadler (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 2, 2020 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining six months of the Congress

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; it was never scheduled for a vote at any point in the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a stage where party positions were recorded in a vote; only 2 of 231 House Democrats cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and police departments
industries.note: The bill would expose police agencies and prosecutors' offices to more federal investigations, new state-led lawsuits, and binding reform agreements, and would remove a 2018 DOJ policy that limited consent decrees. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against communities seeking accountability for civil rights violations.

industries.industry: Police unions and law enforcement advocacy groups
industries.note: Consent decrees and pattern-or-practice suits constrain union-negotiated disciplinary and operational practices. The bill's expanded enforcement would have increased pressure on those arrangements. (Their role in the bill's fate is not shown in the provided record.)
